topic: Non-Constitutional Bodies: NITI Aayog, NHRC, and CBI
description: Non-Constitutional Bodies in Indian Polity are institutions that are not mentioned in the Constitution of India. They are established either by an Act of Parliament (Statutory Bodies) or by an executive resolution of the government (Executive/Extra-Constitutional Bodies).

sections.title: Classification of Non-Constitutional Bodies
sections.description: Non-constitutional bodies are primarily classified into two main categories based on their method of establishment and legal backing.

key_concepts.explanation: Institutions created by an Act of Parliament or a State Legislature. They derive their powers from the specific law passed. Example: National Human Rights Commission (NHRC).
Institutions established merely by an executive resolution or cabinet decision without any legislative backing. Example: NITI Aayog.

sections.title: NITI Aayog
sections.description: NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India) is the premier policy 'Think Tank' of the Government of India, providing both directional and policy inputs.

key_concepts.explanation: The guiding principle of NITI Aayog, which ensures that the Centre and the States work together as equal partners for national development.
Unlike the top-down model of the former Planning Commission, NITI Aayog formulates plans at the village level and aggregates them progressively at higher levels of government.

historical_events.significance: It replaced the 65-year-old Planning Commission to better serve the needs and aspirations of a changing India.

key_associations.extra_info: The Prime Minister serves as the ex-officio Chairperson of the NITI Aayog.

key_associations.associated_with: CMs of all States and Lt. Governors of UTs
key_associations.extra_info: This council embodies the spirit of cooperative federalism by involving states in decision-making.

sections.title: National Human Rights Commission (NHRC)
sections.description: The NHRC is the national watchdog of human rights, responsible for the protection and promotion of rights relating to life, liberty, equality, and dignity of the individual.

historical_events.significance: Formed as a statutory body under the provisions of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.

important_facts.fact: The Chairperson of the NHRC must be a retired Chief Justice of India or a Judge of the Supreme Court.
Following the 2019 amendment, the tenure of the Chairperson and members is 3 years or until they attain the age of 70 years, whichever is earlier.
The Commission possesses the powers of a civil court, but its recommendations are advisory in nature and not legally binding on the government.

sections.title: Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI)
sections.description: The CBI is the premier investigating agency of the Central Government, primarily handling cases related to corruption, economic offences, and special crimes.

historical_events.significance: Set up via a resolution of the Ministry of Home Affairs. It was later transferred to the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions.

key_associations.extra_info: The committee on prevention of corruption strongly recommended the establishment of the CBI.
The CBI is not a statutory body; it derives its investigative powers and jurisdiction from the DSPE Act.

important_facts.fact: The Director of the CBI is appointed on the recommendation of a three-member committee consisting of the Prime Minister (Chairperson), the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha, and the Chief Justice of India.
The CBI Director is provided with a security of tenure of not less than 2 years under the Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) Act, 2003.
